html:
A 1966 film by the Senegalese writer and director Ousmane Sembène, often called the first feature film made in sub-Saharan Africa by an African director. Its French title is La Noire de..., "the Black girl of...", as if she belonged to someone.

Diouana, a young woman from Dakar, takes a job as a nanny with a French couple and follows them to the French Riviera. There she is treated as a maid and a curiosity, cut off from everyone, and stripped of her dignity. The story ends in her suicide. Sembène based it on his own short story, inspired by a real news report.

Shot in black and white, the film turns the gaze of colonial cinema around: here the French are the strange ones, seen by an African. Sembène, a former docker in Marseille and the author of God's Bits of Wood, is known as the father of African cinema. Black Girl won France's Prix Jean Vigo in 1966, and Sembène's later films made Senegal a centre of African cinema, celebrated at festivals such as FESPACO.
